paragraphs.heading: A ring of rubble
paragraphs.text: The asteroid belt is a doughnut-shaped zone that circles the Sun, lying roughly between the paths of Mars and Jupiter. It holds a huge number of solid, lumpy bodies called asteroids, also known as minor planets. Astronomers often call it the main belt, to tell it apart from other groups of asteroids elsewhere in the Solar System. Of all the circumstellar discs in the Solar System, it is the innermost and the smallest.

paragraphs.heading: Mostly empty space
paragraphs.text: Its objects come in many sizes, but every one is far smaller than a planet. On average, about a million kilometres separate one from the next. The material is spread so thin that many uncrewed spacecraft have crossed the belt with no trouble at all. Added together, everything in it weighs only about 3% as much as the Moon, and roughly 60% of that sits in four bodies: Ceres, Vesta, Pallas and Hygiea. Ceres, about 950 km across, is the only one big enough to count as a dwarf planet.

paragraphs.heading: A planet that never formed
paragraphs.text: The belt began as a crowd of planetesimals, the small building blocks that came before protoplanets, gathered from the primordial solar nebula. The gravity of Mars and Jupiter stirred them up and gave them too much speed, so instead of joining into a planet, colliding bodies shattered, along with most of the young protoplanets. Within the Solar System's first 100 million years, the belt lost 99.9% of its original mass. Some of the broken pieces later drifted inward and struck the inner planets as meteorites.

paragraphs.heading: Families and gaps
paragraphs.text: Big asteroids still crash into each other, and the pieces can form an asteroid family whose members share similar orbits and makeup. Astronomers sort asteroids by their spectra, and most land in three basic groups: carbon-rich C-type, silicate S-type, and an X-type group that takes in the metal-rich ones. Where an asteroid's time to circle the Sun forms an orbital resonance with Jupiter, Jupiter disturbs it strongly. Asteroids at those distances get swept into other orbits, leaving empty lanes called Kirkwood gaps.

paragraphs.heading: The hunt for a missing planet
paragraphs.text: In 1596 Johannes Kepler predicted that a planet would turn up between Mars and Jupiter, because the space between their orbits looked too large for his model. In 1766 Johann Daniel Titius pointed out a pattern in the spacing of the planets, now called the Titius-Bode Law. Start a list at 0, then 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 and so on, doubling each time; add four to each and divide by 10, and you get the orbit sizes of the planets in astronomical units. The fit only works if a missing planet sits at the 24 slot, between Mars and Jupiter. When William Herschel found Uranus in 1781 and its orbit matched the pattern, some astronomers decided a planet must be hiding in that gap.

paragraphs.heading: Ceres and the first asteroids
paragraphs.text: On January 1, 1801, Giuseppe Piazzi spotted a tiny moving object at exactly the distance the pattern predicted, and named it Ceres after the Roman harvest goddess. About 15 months later Heinrich Olbers found a second one, Pallas, in the same region. Even in the strongest telescopes both stayed points of light rather than showing discs, and apart from their quick motion they looked just like stars. After Karl Ludwig Hencke found a fifth object in 1845, discoveries came faster and faster. In time these bodies were taken off the list of planets, and Herschel's word for them, asteroids, slowly came into everyday use.

paragraphs.heading: A pattern that fell apart
paragraphs.text: The rule that sent astronomers searching did not survive. When Neptune was found in 1846, its orbit was nowhere near where the law said it should be, and scientists stopped trusting it. No one has explained the pattern since, and most astronomers now treat it as a coincidence.
